doc.title: Jim Galloway interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: First night at the Colonial Tavern and the Toronto club circuit
summary: Culture shock and hearing Vic Dickenson, Buster Bailey, Herman Autrey and Red Richards; Dickenson's influence and Toronto's touring circuit.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Cool. Was it any kind of culture shock at all or was it fairly—

Oh yeah, a little bit, a little bit. The first shock was the very first night I arrived. Again, at that time in Glasgow for example, you didn’t go into a bar to hear jazz. They didn’t have music in bars as they have here. And so on my first night in Toronto I was on Yonge Street which is the main drag, and there’s this place I see called the Colonial Tavern. And so I go in there and I literally stopped in my tracks because on the bandstand there was Vic Dickinson, Buster Bailey, Herman Autrey, Red Richards on piano — I thought I’d died and gone to heaven. So that was my first shock.
That was a pretty good affirmation of your decision though I guess. Hey, I did the right thing. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

Yeah. And subsequently — I never worked with Buster, he died shortly after that — but I became very good friends with Vic Dickinson, I’m still a good friend of Red Richards, Herman I’ve played with, he’s unfortunately, well like most of them departed. But Vic was a very huge influence on me. And I find that a lot of my influences have not necessarily been reed players.
Reed players all the time. I learned a huge amount about the business just playing beside people like Vic Dickinson and Bobby Hackett for example.
So Toronto was a stop for those guys on their criss-crossing of the country.

Yeah, at that time there was a reasonable circuit, and clubs could still afford to bring in groups. Travel wasn’t as horrendously expensive as it’s become, and there were traveling groups. And The Colonial and the Town Tavern were the two spots in Toronto in those days that brought in musicians. And I saw a huge procession of great players who would come through the town. Toronto always was a very good jazz town, still is.
They have a big festival up there every year, don’t they?
